young.html: Montesquieu was a French judge and nobleman who spent twenty years on one giant question: why do different countries have different laws?

He decided that good laws must fit the people who live under them: their kind of government, their climate and land, their work, their customs and their religion. A law that works well in one place might fail in another.

He also had a famous idea about keeping people free. Power should not all be in one person's hands. Split it into three: one group makes the laws, one carries them out, and one judges. Then each part can check the others, so no one can become a bully.

young.name: gb-three-powers
young.cap: Give the three powers to different people, or put them in one hand, and see what Montesquieu says happens to freedom.

young.html: Three-part game. Play a simple game where one person makes up the rules, a second person is the referee who decides if the rules were broken, and a third is the scorekeeper. Then play again where one person does all three jobs. Which game feels fairer? Why?

full.html: Charles-Louis de Secondat, Baron de Montesquieu (1689–1755), was a judge in the parliament of Bordeaux. He became famous for the Persian Letters (1721), a satire of French society through the eyes of two Persian visitors, then traveled through Europe and spent nearly two years in England. The Spirit of Laws (1748), in 31 books, was translated into English by Thomas Nugent in 1750. The Catholic Church placed it on its Index of forbidden books in 1751, and it was read and argued over across Europe and America.

full.text: Three kinds of government, three principles

full.html: Montesquieu sorts governments by their nature (who holds power) and their principle (the passion that makes them work):

head: Government
Who rules
Its principle
rows: the people, or part of them
virtue: love of country and of equality
one person, by his own will

full.html: Laws should suit the principle: a republic needs education in public virtue, a monarchy needs ranks and the courts that defend them, and despotism needs little law at all. Later books relate laws to climate (Books XIV–XVII), soil, commerce, religion and population. Many of his claims about climate and national character are now rejected, but the idea that laws must be studied in their whole social setting was new and lasting.

full.text: Liberty and the separation of powers

full.html: Political liberty, Montesquieu says, is not doing whatever one wants, but the security of living under laws, the feeling that one need not be afraid of another citizen. Experience teaches that anyone with power tends to abuse it:

full.text: To prevent this abuse, it is necessary from the very nature of things that power should be a check to power.
full.author: Montesquieu
full.ed: The Spirit of Laws, revised edition, Colonial Press, New York

full.html: In Book XI, ch. 6, describing the constitution of England as he understood it, he names three powers: the legislative, the executive and the power of judging:

full.text: When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, or in the same body of magistrates, there can be no liberty; because apprehensions may arise, lest the same monarch or senate should enact tyrannical laws, to execute them in a tyrannical manner.
full.author: Montesquieu
full.ed: The Spirit of Laws, revised edition, Colonial Press, New York

full.name: gb-three-powers
full.cap: Combine any two powers, or all three, and read Montesquieu's warning for each case.

full.html: He adds that judging should not be joined to either other power, or the judge would be a legislator or an oppressor. He praises England's two-house legislature, the executive's veto and trial by jury. Historians note that his picture of England was partly idealized: the English ministers already sat in Parliament.

Montesquieu thought commerce softens manners and inclines nations to peace. Book XV attacks slavery with bitter irony, listing the "arguments" of slaveholders in a way that exposes them. His constant advice is moderation: sudden, sweeping changes in law are dangerous, and the best laws suit a people as it is.

Thinking Montesquieu invented checks and balances from nothing. He drew on Locke, on ancient writers and on what he saw in England; his gift was to set the three powers out clearly as a rule for liberty.

deep.html: Studies of American political writing in the 1760s–1800s find Montesquieu among the authors the founders cited most. In The Federalist No. 47, Madison calls him "the celebrated Montesquieu" and the "oracle" on separation of powers, and argues that the powers must be separate but not wholly unconnected, so that each can check the others. The Anti-Federalists also cited him, arguing that he showed a republic must be small; Madison's answer in No. 10, on the Federalist rung, is that a large republic can protect liberty better.

Some readers find the book disorderly, with many chapters only a paragraph long. Others criticize its climate theory and its use of travelers' tales about distant peoples. Defenders reply that Montesquieu was among the first to study law as a social science, comparing many societies to find the causes behind their laws.

items: Why might it be dangerous for one person to make, enforce and judge the rules?
Should laws be the same everywhere, or fit each people?
What makes people feel free under a government?

questions: In your family or classroom, who makes the rules, who makes sure they're followed, and who settles arguments?
Why might even a good person misuse power if no one can check it?
Montesquieu said laws should fit the people. Can you think of a rule that fits one place but not another?
What does it mean to feel safe from other people? Why did Montesquieu call that liberty?
Is it better to change laws slowly or quickly? Why?
